beats.headline: Why does scaling your consumer group stall throughput?
beats.subline: It isn't just network lag. It's how Kafka handles partition rebalancing.
beats.narration: Scaling your consumer group should boost performance, but often it causes massive stalls. If you have four partitions and six pods, two pods sit idle. Let's look at why.

beats.title: Partition Ownership Rules
beats.subtitle: One partition, one consumer per group
beats.narration: Within one group, each partition maps to exactly one consumer. If your pod count exceeds your partition count, those extra pods are useless hot standbys. Kafka enforces this to guarantee strict message ordering.

beats.title: The Thread-Safety Trap

steps.explanation: KafkaConsumer is NOT thread-safe. All poll and commit calls must reside on the same thread.
Spring Kafka handles concurrency by spawning separate consumer instances, not sharing one.

beats.narration: Never call poll from multiple threads. KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe. If you need more throughput, spin up separate consumer instances—Spring does this automatically with the concurrency setting.

beats.title: Eager vs. Cooperative Rebalancing
beats.narration: Avoid Eager rebalancing. It stops the world for every pod. Cooperative Sticky Assignor keeps unaffected partitions running while only moving the necessary ones, keeping your pipeline flowing.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Why auto-commit is a data loss trap →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we tackle the dangerous auto-commit default and the hybrid commit pattern for production-grade reliability.

beats.headline: Is your auto-commit losing data?
beats.subline: The default setting is a ticking time bomb for business-critical events.
beats.narration: Auto-commit is the easiest way to lose data. If your app crashes after the commit but before processing finishes, those records are gone forever. Let's fix your commit strategy.

beats.title: Commit Strategies
beats.narration: Sync is safe but slow. Async is fast but lacks retries. Why? Because a late retry could overwrite a newer, successful commit, causing duplicate processing. Always use a hybrid approach.

beats.title: The Hybrid Commit Pattern

steps.explanation: Use async for high-throughput steady-state processing.
Use sync during rebalances to ensure no work is lost before partition handoff.

beats.narration: The production standard: use commitAsync in your loop for speed. But, implement a RebalanceListener to call commitSync when partitions are revoked. This guarantees you finish work before losing the partition.

beats.title: Static Membership
beats.caption: Eliminate rebalances on pod restarts
beats.narration: If you use Kubernetes StatefulSets, set group.instance.id. This lets your pod restart and reclaim its old partitions within the session timeout, bypassing the rebalance storm entirely.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Use hybrid commit (Async loop + Sync revoke)
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): The poison pill loop →
beats.narration: Commits are now safe. In Part 3, we look at poison pills—the malformed records that can wedge your partition in an infinite retry loop.

beats.headline: One bad record can stop your entire service.
beats.subline: Deserialization happens before your code runs. Here is how to survive.
beats.narration: A malformed JSON record is a poison pill. It crashes deserialization inside the poll loop, so your code never even sees it. The consumer retries the same bad record forever.

beats.title: The Poison Pill Loop
beats.subtitle: Why your partition gets wedged
beats.narration: The deserializer runs inside poll. If it fails, the offset never advances. You are stuck in a loop. You need to move that bad record to a Dead Letter Topic.

beats.title: ErrorHandlingDeserializer

steps.explanation: Wraps your real deserializer to catch errors without crashing the thread.
Routes the poison pill to a separate topic so the main queue can keep moving.

beats.narration: Use ErrorHandlingDeserializer. It catches the exception and passes a null payload to your listener. Then, use a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer to push that bad record to a DLT, allowing your partition to advance.

beats.title: Timeout Tuning
beats.caption: Don't let slow processing trigger rebalances
beats.narration: If your processing is slow, your poll interval will expire. Drop max.poll.records to 50. This ensures you finish batches faster, keeping your consumer inside the group and avoiding unnecessary rebalances.

beats.narration: Poison pills are handled. In Part 4, we look at the next-gen rebalance protocol that moves assignment to the broker, effectively killing the rebalance problem.

beats.headline: Rebalances are finally getting fixed.
beats.subline: KIP-848 moves the heavy lifting from the client to the broker.
beats.narration: Rebalances have been a pain for years. KIP-848 changes the game by moving partition assignment to the broker. No more group leader, no more synchronization barriers.

beats.title: KIP-848 Architecture
beats.subtitle: Broker-side assignment
beats.narration: In the new protocol, the broker does all the work. Clients just send heartbeats. The coordinator pushes incremental updates to each member, making rebalances continuous and non-blocking.

beats.title: Enable KIP-848
beats.caption: The new consumer protocol
beats.narration: Just set group.protocol to consumer. You no longer need to manage strategies on every client. It's production-ready in Kafka 4.0 and it's the future of scalable event streaming.

beats.title: Classic vs. New Protocol
beats.narration: The classic way requires clients to agree on the state. The new way is server-driven. It's faster, simpler, and makes large-scale consumer groups much more stable.

takeaways: KIP-848 moves assignment to the broker
